title: System Design Interview Field Guide
description: A system-design field guide built around requirements pressure, read/write paths, component justification, reliability, and trade-off closure.

sections.title: Mental Model: Pressure Before Components
sections.summary: A system design interview is a pressure-mapping exercise. Requirements create pressure; pressure creates architecture.
items: Start by identifying users, core actions, scale, latency, availability, consistency, retention, and regions.
Convert vague product scope into one write path and one read path.
Only add a component when a named pressure forces it.
For every component, say why it exists, what state it owns, how it scales, and how it fails.
End by proving the design meets the requirements and naming the biggest remaining trade-off.

sections.title: Cheatsheet: Scale Signals
sections.summary: Use rough math to decide which pressures are real enough to change the architecture.
items: Average QPS = daily requests / 86,400; peak QPS is usually 3x to 10x average unless the prompt says otherwise.
Storage/day = writes/day * average object size; include replication and retention when storage is large.
Bandwidth/sec = QPS * payload size; separate read and write bandwidth for media-heavy systems.
Cache memory = hot keys * average cached value size * overhead factor 1.2 to 2.
Partition count rough cut = max(storage / target shard size, peak QPS / target shard QPS).
Availability: 99.9% allows 43.8 min/month; 99.99% allows 4.38 min/month; 99.999% allows 26 sec/month.

sections.title: Cheatsheet: Decision Moves
sections.summary: Use these moves when the interviewer asks why a component belongs in the design.
items: Cache: use for hot repeated reads or expensive recompute; name TTL, invalidation, stampede control, and fallback.
Queue: use for bursty or slow side effects; name idempotent workers, retry budget, DLQ, and lag metric.
Storage: choose from access pattern; name entities, primary keys, indexes, shard key, and retention.
Search index: use for text/ranking/filter queries; name async indexing and freshness delay.
CDN/object storage: use for global static/media reads; name cache headers, purge path, and access control.
Reliability: pick one failure, mitigation, metric, and recovery path instead of listing every possible failure.

title: System Design Interview Strategy
description: A concrete timeline and script for running the system design round.

sections.title: 45-Minute Timeline
sections.summary: Keep the round on rails.
items: 0-5 min: clarify users, features, non-goals, scale, SLOs, consistency.
5-10 min: APIs and data model. Do not draw services before entities.
10-20 min: simple high-level architecture with read and write paths.
20-32 min: deep dive one bottleneck: feed fanout, search, storage, cache invalidation, ranking, or reliability.
32-40 min: failure modes: retries, idempotency, backpressure, failover, data recovery, observability.
40-45 min: summarize requirements met, trade-offs, and next improvements.

sections.title: Board Layout
sections.summary: Use a predictable drawing layout so the interviewer can follow you.
items: Top left: requirements and non-goals.
Top right: numbers: QPS, storage/day, peak multiplier, latency/SLO.
Middle: boxes for client, gateway, services, data stores, caches, queues, workers.
Bottom left: data model with keys and indexes.
Bottom right: failure modes and trade-offs.
Use arrows labeled with verbs: createPost, readFeed, invalidateCache, publishEvent.

sections.title: Useful Phrases
sections.summary: Concrete lines that show senior judgment.
items: 'I will keep v1 simple and add this component only when the scale math requires it.'
'The key correctness risk here is duplicate writes, so I want an idempotency key.'
'This cache improves p95 reads, but I need an invalidation or TTL story.'
'This is eventually consistent; the user-visible stale window is acceptable because...'
'If this becomes a hot-key problem, I would split by [key] or add request coalescing.'
'The biggest unresolved trade-off is [latency vs consistency/cost/complexity].'

title: Requirements and Estimation
description: Concrete requirement prompts, formulas, and sizing shortcuts.

sections.title: Requirement Prompts
sections.summary: Ask questions that change the architecture.
items: Feed/timeline: fanout on write or read? following count distribution? celebrity users? freshness?
Chat: one-to-one or groups? ordering guarantee? offline delivery? read receipts? media?
URL shortener: custom aliases? expiry? analytics? abusive links? redirect latency?
Search: exact match, prefix, typo tolerance, filters, ranking freshness, permissions?
File/video: upload size, resumable upload, transcoding, thumbnails, CDN, access control?
Payments/booking: idempotency, reservation timeout, double spend, audit log, reconciliation?

sections.title: Fast Formulas
sections.summary: Use approximate math aloud.
items: DAU * actions/user/day = daily operations.
Daily operations / 86,400 = average QPS.
Average QPS * 5 = reasonable peak QPS unless prompt gives spikes.
Writes/day * object size = raw storage/day.
Raw storage * replication factor * retention days = storage footprint.
Read QPS * response size = outbound bandwidth.
Index size often 20-100% of raw data; call it out when storage is large.

sections.title: SLO Cheats
sections.summary: Translate quality targets into design choices.
items: p95 < 100ms: cache, precompute, local region, avoid fanout on read.
p95 < 1s: DB plus cache/search is usually acceptable.
99.99% availability: multi-AZ, health checks, failover, graceful degradation.
Strong consistency: single writer/transactional DB/consensus cost; lower availability during partitions.
Eventual consistency: async queues, replicas, cache; explain stale window and reconciliation.
High durability: replication, backups, checksums, object storage, restore drills.

title: Core Components Cheat Sheet
description: When to use common system components and what trade-off to mention.

sections.title: Component Decision Rules
sections.summary: Only add a component when it solves a named pressure.
items: Load balancer: distribute traffic, health check instances, support rolling deploys.
API gateway: auth, rate limits, routing, request shaping, not business logic.
Cache: repeated reads, expensive computation, hot objects; mention TTL/invalidation.
Queue: absorb spikes, decouple slow work, retry safely; mention idempotent workers and DLQ.
Stream: durable ordered event log, replay, multiple consumers; mention partition key.
CDN: static/media/global reads; mention cache headers and purge path.
Search index: text/ranking/filter queries; mention async indexing and freshness delay.
Coordinator/lock: leader election or exclusive work; mention lease expiry and fencing tokens.

sections.title: Cache Patterns
sections.summary: Choose a cache strategy explicitly.
items: Cache-aside: app checks cache, loads DB on miss, writes cache. Simple and common.
Write-through: write cache and DB together. Safer reads, higher write latency.
Write-behind: write cache/queue first, DB later. Fast but data-loss risk.
TTL only: acceptable for stale-tolerant data; simple but can stampede.
Invalidation: delete/update key on write; hard when many derived keys exist.
Stampede controls: jitter TTL, request coalescing, background refresh, single-flight lock.

sections.title: Queue and Worker Patterns
sections.summary: Queues add reliability concerns you must name.
items: Use idempotency key per job to survive retries.
Use DLQ for poison messages after max attempts.
Use exponential backoff for transient downstream failures.
Use partition key for ordering per user/order/chat, not global ordering.
Use visibility timeout or leases so stuck workers release work.
Track lag, retry count, age of oldest message, and worker error rate.

title: Data and Storage Cheat Sheet
description: Concrete storage choices, keys, indexes, sharding, and consistency patterns.

sections.title: Storage Choice Rules
sections.summary: Pick storage from access pattern, not fashion.
items: Relational DB: transactions, joins, constraints, payments, bookings, metadata.
Key-value store: get/put by key, sessions, counters, feature flags, simple cache-like data.
Document store: flexible nested objects, user profiles, product documents, low join need.
Wide-column store: huge write volume, time-series, event tables, predictable partition key.
Object storage: blobs, images, videos, logs, backups; store metadata separately.
Search engine: inverted index, ranking, filtering, typo/prefix; not source of truth.
Graph DB: relationship traversal depth matters and cannot be precomputed cheaply.

sections.title: Keys and Indexes
sections.summary: Name primary key and query indexes out loud.
items: Primary key should match most common direct lookup: userId, postId, orderId, shortCode.
Composite index order matters: equality fields first, then range/sort field.
Feed table: partition by userId, sort by createdAt desc.
Chat messages: partition by conversationId, sort by messageSequence or createdAt.
Time-series: partition by entityId plus time bucket to avoid unbounded partitions.
Unique constraint: username, email, shortCode, idempotencyKey per user/order.
Secondary indexes speed reads but slow writes and add storage; mention write amplification.

sections.title: Sharding and Consistency
sections.summary: Be precise about partition keys and stale data.
items: Shard by userId when user-owned data dominates and cross-user queries are rare.
Shard by objectId for uniform object lookup; add indexes for owner queries.
Avoid hot partitions: celebrity user, global counter, trending hashtag, current timestamp bucket.
Use consistent hashing when nodes change often; use directory service when placement needs control.
Strong consistency: use transactions/single leader/quorum; cost is latency and failover complexity.
Eventual consistency: use async events, reconciliation jobs, versioning, and user-visible stale tolerance.
Conflict resolution: last-write-wins, version vector, server timestamp, manual review, or domain-specific merge.

title: Trade-offs and Reliability
description: Failure-mode playbooks and trade-off language for senior system design rounds.

sections.title: Failure Mode Menu
sections.summary: Pick the relevant failures before the interviewer asks.
items: Duplicate write: idempotency key, unique constraint, dedupe table.
Partial failure: transactional boundary, saga, compensating action, retry policy.
Queue backlog: autoscale workers, shed noncritical work, priority queues, backpressure.
Cache outage: bypass to DB with rate limits, degrade features, warm critical keys.
DB primary failure: replica promotion, write pause, read-only mode, RPO/RTO statement.
Hot key: key splitting, local cache, request coalescing, precompute, async fanout.
Thundering herd: jittered TTL, token bucket, single-flight, circuit breaker.
Data corruption: checksums, audit log, backups, restore drills, dual-write verification.

sections.title: Reliability Patterns
sections.summary: Know the pattern and the risk it creates.
items: Retry: handles transient failure; risk duplicate side effects.
Timeout: prevents resource exhaustion; risk false failure if too aggressive.
Circuit breaker: protects downstream; risk degraded user experience.
Bulkhead: isolates failures by pool/tenant/feature; risk underutilized capacity.
Rate limit: protects system and abuse; risk blocking legitimate spikes.
Graceful degradation: preserve core path while disabling recommendations, analytics, thumbnails, or notifications.
Outbox pattern: write DB row and event atomically, worker publishes later.
Saga: distributed workflow with compensating actions when transaction cannot span services.

sections.title: Trade-off Language
sections.summary: Use explicit A versus B statements.
items: Cache: lower latency and DB load versus stale reads and invalidation complexity.
Queue: smoother spikes and retries versus delayed processing and duplicate handling.
Sharding: higher capacity versus cross-shard query and operational complexity.
Replication: higher availability and read scale versus lag and failover complexity.
Precompute: faster reads versus slower writes and storage cost.
Fanout on write: fast reads versus expensive writes for high-fanout users.
Fanout on read: cheap writes versus slow reads for users following many accounts.

title: System Design Practice Playbook
description: Reusable templates for common system design prompts and timed practice.

sections.title: Prompt Templates
sections.summary: Use these known decompositions during practice.
items: URL shortener: encode/create shortCode, redirect read path, custom alias, expiry, analytics async.
News feed: follow graph, post write, fanout strategy, ranking, cache feed, celebrity handling.
Chat: conversation/message model, websocket gateway, ordering, offline queue, push notification.
Video upload: pre-signed URL, object storage, metadata DB, transcode queue, CDN, playback manifest.
Search: source DB, indexing pipeline, inverted index, ranking, filters, freshness delay.
Rate limiter: key choice, token bucket/leaky bucket, Redis or local counters, distributed consistency.
Booking/payment: reservation lock, idempotency, expiry, payment state machine, audit log.

sections.title: Deep-Dive Prompts
sections.summary: Ask yourself these after drawing v1.
items: What is the hottest key or endpoint?
Which operation must be strongly consistent?
What happens if this request is retried three times?
Which data can be stale and for how long?
What is the first bottleneck at 10x traffic?
What metric alerts before users complain?
How do we backfill or migrate this schema?
What is the cheapest graceful degradation mode?

sections.title: Practice Loop
sections.summary: A concrete 60-minute solo session.
items: 5 min: scope and numbers only.
10 min: APIs and data model.
15 min: read/write architecture.
15 min: one deep dive with trade-offs.
10 min: failure modes and observability.
5 min: record missed questions, bad assumptions, and one improved phrase.
